```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", message = FALSE)
```

[Model diagnostics](model-checking.html)
explains the shared diagnostic methods. This article applies them to models
with changing variance, exact zeros, censoring and categorical responses. In
each case, the response distribution determines how residuals and replicated
observations should be calculated. The examples use {mgcv} for fitting,
{gratia} for diagnostics and {ggplot2} for plotting. The motorcycle data come
from {MASS}, and the second fit to these data uses {GJRM}.

```{r packages}
library("gratia")
load_mgcv()
library("ggplot2")
```

## Fit a Gaussian model with changing variance

The `MASS::mcycle` data record head acceleration after a simulated motorcycle
impact. The mean acceleration changes rapidly after impact, and
its spread also appears to vary. A constant-variance Gaussian model can
represent the mean while failing to capture that spread.

The fits assume independent measurement errors. The available columns, time
and acceleration, provide no accident identifiers for estimating correlation
between measurements from the same accident. We plot the observations and
start with a model that allows mean acceleration to vary smoothly with time
but assumes constant variance:

```{r impact-data}
data("mcycle", package = "MASS")
ggplot(mcycle, aes(times, accel)) + geom_point() +
  labs(x = "Time after impact (ms)", y = "Acceleration (g)")
constant <- gam(accel ~ s(times, k = 20), data = mcycle, method = "REML")
```

Next we use `gaulss()` to let both the mean and standard deviation vary with
time. We plot its two smooths and compare the diagnostics with those from
the constant-variance model:

```{r impact-scale}
varying <- gam(list(accel ~ s(times, k = 20), ~ s(times, k = 6)),
  data = mcycle, family = gaulss(), method = "REML")
draw(varying)
appraise(constant, type = "quantile", seed = 401)
appraise(varying, type = "quantile", seed = 401)
```

The first smooth contributes to mean acceleration. The second contributes to
the predictor for the standard deviation. For `gaulss()`, the inverse link
returns the reciprocal standard deviation. We take its reciprocal to plot
the fitted standard deviation in the original units.

```{r impact-sd}
impact_grid <- data.frame(times = seq(min(mcycle$times), max(mcycle$times),
  length.out = 100))
eta <- predict(varying, newdata = impact_grid, type = "link")
inverse_sd <- inv_link(varying, parameter = "scale")(eta[, 2])
ggplot(data.frame(impact_grid, sd = 1 / inverse_sd), aes(times, sd)) +
  geom_line() + labs(x = "Time after impact (ms)", y = "Fitted standard deviation (g)")
```

The spread increases around the period of rapid change. Modelling it reduces a
systematic residual pattern and describes how both mean acceleration and its
spread change with time after impact.

### Estimate means and variability

`fitted_moments()` calculates quantities such as the response mean, variance
and standard deviation from the fitted distribution parameters. It uses the
joint uncertainty in those parameters. We evaluate all three quantities at
three times after impact so that the output shows each quantity.

```{r impact-moments}
fitted_moments(varying, data = data.frame(times = c(10, 25, 45)),
  moments = c("mean", "variance", "sd"))
```

Each `.parameter` identifies a requested quantity. For variance rows, `.fitted`
contains the estimated response variance, and `.se` describes uncertainty in
that estimate. Standard errors and interval bounds are on the quantity's own
scale. By default the delta method approximates how changes in the model
parameters affect each quantity and accounts for their covariance.

`conditional_moments()` builds the same covariate grid as `conditional_values()`.
Other covariates are held at their typical values. Choose posterior simulation
to evaluate the moments at joint parameter draws, then summarise those values:

```{r impact-conditional-moments}
conditional_moments(varying, condition = "times", moments = c("mean", "sd"),
  uncertainty = "simulation", n_draws = 1000, seed = 419) |>
  draw()
```

Other available quantities are the coefficient of variation (`"cv"`),
skewness, kurtosis and excess kurtosis; `moments = "all"` requests all seven.
CV requires a positive mean, so it is inappropriate where predicted
acceleration is negative.

For models with a global dispersion or shape parameter, the default
`nuisance = "estimated"` includes its uncertainty where the fitting method
provides the required information. Use `nuisance = "fixed"` to hold such
parameters at their estimates. Parameters modelled by coefficients, including
the changing scale in this example, retain their joint uncertainty.

Some distributions have undefined moments for particular parameter values.
These results carry a `.status` explaining the problem. With simulation,
`.p_defined` records the proportion of draws with a defined moment; an interval
is withheld if any draw is undefined. See `fitted_moments()` for the supported
families and uncertainty calculations.

Finally, compare the observed acceleration distribution with replicated
datasets. This check draws the mean and scale coefficients together, retaining
their covariance. The smoothing parameters stay fixed at their fitted values
in this check. If a GAM estimates dispersion or shape outside the coefficient
vector, the check also holds those parameters fixed.

```{r impact-ppc}
posterior_predictive_plot(varying, n = 50, seed = 402)
```

This check compares the overall acceleration distributions, pooling
measurements across time. Use the residual-versus-predictor panels above to
see whether the model captures changes in spread after impact.

### Fit the mean and standard deviation with GJRM

Fit the same two smooths using `GJRM::gamlss()`, which estimates their
smoothness with a different fitting procedure. Then plot the smooths and
check the fitted Gaussian distribution.

```{r gjrm-impact}
library("GJRM")
impact_gjrm <- GJRM::gamlss(list(accel ~ s(times, k = 20), ~ s(times, k = 6)),
  data = mcycle, family = "N")
gratia::draw(impact_gjrm)
appraise(impact_gjrm, seed = 403)
posterior_predictive_plot(impact_gjrm, n = 50, seed = 404)
```

The smooth subtitles show which distribution parameter each curve describes.
Compare the quantile residuals and posterior predictive checks with those from
the mgcv fit to see whether the two fits show similar departures.

These diagnostics also support several other uncensored univariate GJRM
families, including Poisson, negative binomial, beta, Gamma and Weibull.
See [`diagnostic_support`](../reference/diagnostic_support.html) for the full
list. For some joint models fitted with `GJRM::gjrm()`, gratia can check each
response distribution separately. The help topic specifies which model
structures and diagnostic functions are supported.

For Weibull fits, the first predictor controls scale rather than the response
mean. For logistic and Gumbel fits it controls location; a Gumbel location is
also different from its mean. gratia calculates response means and variances
from both fitted parameters for observed-versus-fitted and Pearson residual
plots. Posterior predictive checks draw both equations' coefficients together,
so uncertainty in both equations contributes to the replicated responses.

All these families support PIT, quantile, response and Pearson residuals,
as well as simulation-based residuals in the style of {DHARMa}. These work in
ordinary and scalable plots. Deviance residuals are available for
Gaussian (`"N"`), Gamma (`"GA"` or `"GAi"`) and Poisson (`"P"`) fits. For
example, a fitted beta model `beta_fit` can be checked with
`appraise(beta_fit, seed = 405)` or
`appraise(beta_fit, ppcheck = TRUE, n_ppc = 50, seed = 405)`.
To simulate a QQ reference for Pearson residuals, use
`qq_plot(beta_fit, type = "pearson", method = "simulate", seed = 405)`.
The default quantile residuals instead use a fixed standard-normal reference.

## Positive observations and precision weights

Suppose a chemical concentration is measured in samples with different amounts
of replication. Averaging more independent measurements can reduce variance
without changing the mean. We simulate positive concentrations whose squared
coefficient of variation is `0.4 / precision`, with a mean that changes
smoothly with flow:

```{r positive-simulation}
set.seed(405)
chemical <- data.frame(flow = runif(400, 0, 10),
  precision = rep(c(1, 2, 4, 8), length.out = 400))
mu <- exp(1 + 0.5 * sin(chemical$flow / 3))
chemical$concentration <- rgamma(400, shape = chemical$precision / 0.4,
  scale = mu * 0.4 / chemical$precision)
```

We fit a smooth flow effect with a Gamma family and log link, supplying the
precision weights so the fitted variance reflects the different amounts of
replication. We then inspect the quantile residual diagnostics:

```{r positive-data}
gamma_fit <- gam(concentration ~ s(flow, k = 10), data = chemical,
  weights = precision, family = Gamma(link = "log"), method = "REML")
appraise(gamma_fit, type = "quantile", seed = 406)
```

The diagnostics and simulations use each observation's weight to calculate
its response distribution. The fitted variance is
$\phi\mu_i^2/w_i$, where $w_i$ is precision and $\phi$ is estimated dispersion.
A larger weight narrows the response distribution. Supplying weights when
sampling with gratia replaces the fitting weights, so use values appropriate
to the measurements you want to simulate.

An inverse Gaussian alternative uses variance $\phi\mu_i^3/w_i$. It therefore
allows variability to increase more rapidly with the mean. Fit it to the same
data and compare the tails of the residual plots.

```{r inverse-gaussian}
ig_fit <- gam(concentration ~ s(flow, k = 10), data = chemical,
  weights = precision, family = inverse.gaussian(link = "log"), method = "REML")
qq_plot(ig_fit, type = "quantile", seed = 406)
worm_plot(ig_fit, method = "uniform", seed = 407)
```

Both models can fit similar means while predicting different tails. In this
example, the data were generated from the Gamma distribution, so the Gamma
fit provides a reference for comparison.

## Check responses with exact zeros and positive amounts

Biomass, rainfall amounts and expenditure can have exact zeros together with
positive continuous observations. A Tweedie distribution with power between
one and two describes the sum of a Poisson-distributed number of positive
Gamma amounts. The sum is zero when that number is zero. The model
links the zero probability and positive distribution through the mean,
dispersion and power. A delta model instead estimates separate occurrence and
positive components. See [Working with sdmTMB models in gratia](sdmTMB-support.html).
We simulate rainfall amounts whose expected value increases with elevation:

```{r tweedie-data}
set.seed(408)
rain <- data.frame(elevation = runif(400, 0, 1))
rain$amount <- mgcv::rTweedie(exp(-0.6 + 1.5 * rain$elevation), p = 1.5, phi = 1)
```

We fit a Tweedie model and compare its residual diagnostics and replicated
response distributions:

```{r tweedie}
rain_fit <- gam(amount ~ s(elevation, k = 10), data = rain,
  family = tw(), method = "REML")
qq_plot(rain_fit, seed = 409)
appraise(rain_fit, type = "quantile", seed = 409)
posterior_predictive_plot(rain_fit, n = 50, seed = 410)
```

For PIT residuals, gratia evaluates the cumulative distribution function
(CDF) of the fitted Poisson–Gamma mixture. At zero, it draws a uniform value
between zero and the fitted probability of a zero. For traditional Tweedie
residuals, the default QQ reference uses simulation to avoid calculating the
inverse CDF, which can be slow for large datasets.

The posterior predictive plot smooths the zeros into a peak with the kernel
density estimate. To check the zeros directly, compare their expected and
observed proportions. We also check that every PIT residual for a zero falls
within its allowed range.

```{r zero-mass}
p <- rain_fit$family$getTheta(TRUE)
phi <- summary(rain_fit)$scale
zero_probability <- exp(-fitted(rain_fit)^(2 - p) / (phi * (2 - p)))
zero_pit <- quantile_residuals(rain_fit, type = "pit", seed = 409)
data.frame(observed_zero_fraction = mean(rain$amount == 0),
  fitted_zero_fraction = mean(zero_probability),
  largest_zero_probability_rank = max(zero_pit[rain$amount == 0] /
    zero_probability[rain$amount == 0]))
```

Dividing a zero's PIT residual by its fitted probability of zero gives a
number between zero and one.

## Observations below a detection limit

A nondetect tells us that the latent concentration lies below a threshold.
Treating the threshold as an exact observation discards that information.
Instead, we record the threshold together with a bound indicating that the
true value is smaller. To demonstrate the encoding we simulate normally
distributed log concentrations. Their mean increases with dose, and independent
Gaussian errors have standard deviation 0.7. We record exact measurements
above a fixed limit and censored measurements below it. For `cnorm()`, record
the detection limit in the first column and `-Inf` in the second for a
nondetect. Repeat exact readings in both columns.

```{r censored-data}
set.seed(411)
assay <- data.frame(dose = runif(300, 0, 4))
latent <- rnorm(300, mean = 0.3 + 0.5 * assay$dose, sd = 0.7)
limit <- 0.6
assay$reading <- pmax(latent, limit)
assay$bound <- ifelse(latent < limit, -Inf, latent)
```

We fit a smooth dose effect with `cnorm()`, using the two response columns
to retain the information in censored observations:

```{r censored}
censored_fit <- gam(cbind(reading, bound) ~ s(dose, k = 8), data = assay,
  family = cnorm(), method = "REML")
```

We now calculate PIT residuals, draw their quantile QQ plot, and plot the PIT
values against dose, distinguishing censored and exact observations:

```{r censored-checks}
u <- quantile_residuals(censored_fit, type = "pit", seed = 412)
qq_plot(censored_fit, type = "quantile", seed = 412)
ggplot(data.frame(assay, pit = u), aes(dose, pit)) +
  geom_point(aes(colour = bound == -Inf)) +
  labs(x = "Dose", y = "PIT residual", colour = "Below limit")
```

An exact observation uses the fitted probability of a response at or below
its measured value. A nondetect draws uniformly from zero to the probability
of falling below the detection limit. For right or interval censoring, the
range is determined by the supplied bounds. `cpois()` and `clog()` have
corresponding count and logistic latent
families. Their distribution helpers and predictions are also supported.
Censored response draws describe the latent response. A posterior predictive
plot of the observed censored values remains unsupported: it needs an explicit
censoring process applied to each draw. For a known fixed limit, you can draw
latent responses and apply that threshold yourself to reproduce the
measurement mechanism.

## Check binomial and categorical responses

Binomial sampling weights have a different meaning from precision weights:
they count trials. A numeric success proportion with 20 trials can take values
in steps of 1/20; a factor-valued Bernoulli response still has one binary trial,
even if it carries likelihood weights. Gratia preserves this distinction in
residuals and response draws. Here we simulate detections at sites with
different visit totals. Detection probability increases with cover, and each
site's success count follows a binomial distribution:

```{r trials-data}
set.seed(413)
visits <- data.frame(cover = runif(240), trials = rep(c(5, 10, 20), 80))
visits$success <- rbinom(240, visits$trials, plogis(-1 + 2 * visits$cover))
visits$failure <- visits$trials - visits$success
```

We fit the successes and failures with a binomial GAM, then inspect residual
and posterior predictive checks:

```{r trials}
visit_fit <- gam(cbind(success, failure) ~ s(cover, k = 8), data = visits,
  family = binomial(), method = "REML")
appraise(visit_fit, type = "quantile", seed = 414)
posterior_predictive_plot(visit_fit, n = 50, seed = 414)
```

The generating probability has a linear logit, so a familiar ordinary logistic
regression also answers this question. The same public diagnostics accept its
`glm` object directly:

```{r ordinary-logistic-model}
visit_glm <- glm(cbind(success, failure) ~ cover, data = visits,
  family = binomial())
qq_plot(visit_glm, type = "quantile", seed = 414)
```

The smooth model allows the log odds to curve with cover. The QQ plots for
both fits look similar, consistent with the linear relationship used to
generate the log odds.

The PIT randomisation uses the probability of the site's observed success
count. The posterior predictive plot uses each site's success proportion,
giving every site equal weight. Sites with 20 visits have less variable
success proportions than sites with five visits at the same fitted detection
probability.

### Ordered response categories

An ordinal model can describe an ordered response, such as a four-level
condition score, by placing thresholds on an underlying continuous variable.
We use gratia's `"eg1"` example with four independent covariates. The latent
response combines nonlinear effects of `x0`, `x1` and `x2` with standard
logistic noise. `x3` has no true effect. Thresholds at -1, 3 and 7 produce
four categories.

```{r ordinal-data}
ordinal_data <- data_sim("eg1", n = 400, dist = "ocat", n_cat = 4,
  cuts = c(-1, 3, 7), seed = 415)
```

We fit a smooth for each covariate with an ordinal family containing four
categories, then check the quantile residuals:

```{r ordinal}
ordinal_fit <- gam(y ~ s(x0) + s(x1) + s(x2) + s(x3), data = ordinal_data,
  family = ocat(R = 4), method = "REML")
qq_plot(ordinal_fit, type = "quantile", seed = 416)
```

The thresholds define the simulated rating process. Quantile residuals
randomise within the probability of each observed category before applying
the standard-normal transformation.

### Nominal response categories

For unordered categories, `mgcv::multinom()` models outcomes coded
`0, ..., K`. To calculate PIT residuals, gratia accumulates probabilities in
that coding order and randomises within the probability of the observed
category. This is the randomised probability transform described by
[Brockwell (2007)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2211730/).
For the same fitted probabilities, changing their accumulation order can
change individual residuals and the patterns they reveal.

We illustrate this with three equally probable categories and a covariate
that has no effect on their probabilities:

```{r multinomial-data}
set.seed(417)
category_data <- data.frame(x = runif(300))
category_data$y <- sample(0:2, nrow(category_data), replace = TRUE)
```

We fit the three-category response with two smooth predictors, then inspect
a quantile QQ plot:

```{r multinomial}
category_fit <- gam(list(y ~ s(x), ~s(x)), data = category_data,
  family = multinom(K = 2), method = "REML")
qq_plot(category_fit, type = "quantile", seed = 418)
```

### Surrogate residuals for nominal categories

Surrogate residuals offer another way to check a `multinom()` model without
accumulating probabilities in a category order. They treat each category as
having an unobserved score, or *utility*, with the highest score determining
the observed choice. gratia draws these scores conditional on that choice,
then subtracts their fitted locations and the Gumbel mean. The construction
follows [Cheng, Wang and Zhang (2021)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8018589/).

In the next simulation, category 0 has a constant score location, category 1's
location increases with `x`, and category 2's decreases. Independent Gumbel
noise creates variation in the choices at each covariate value:

```{r nominal-surrogate-data}
set.seed(417)
nominal_data <- data.frame(x = runif(400, -2, 2))
locations <- cbind(0, nominal_data$x, -.5 - nominal_data$x)
utilities <- locations - log(-log(matrix(runif(1200), nrow = 400)))
nominal_data$y <- max.col(utilities) - 1L
```

We fit a multinomial GAM, extract surrogate residuals for its categories,
and plot the diagnostics:

```{r nominal-surrogate}
nominal_fit <- gam(list(y ~ s(x, k = 6), ~ s(x, k = 6)),
  data = nominal_data, family = multinom(K = 2), method = "REML")
head(surrogate_residuals(nominal_fit, seed = 418))
appraise(nominal_fit, type = "surrogate", seed = 418)
```

`surrogate_residuals()` returns one column per category, including reference
category 0. QQ and worm plots show each category separately against centred Gumbel
quantiles. Their pointwise bands treat fitted parameters as fixed and apply
separately to each component. Residual-versus-fitted panels use each category's
fitted probability, including category 0. Observed-versus-fitted panels compare
category indicators with those probabilities. All panels share a single draw.
For large datasets, `scalable = TRUE` summarises each category separately while
retaining the same residual draws for the same seed. See `surrogate_residuals()`
for the calculation and reference distributions.

## Choose diagnostics for other response families

Other supported response families use the same diagnostic functions. The
following table identifies features of their fitted distributions that matter
when interpreting the results:

| Family or model | What changes in the checks? |
|---|---|
| `gaulss()`, `gammals()`, `gumbls()`, `gevlss()`, `ziplss()` | CDF and quantile references use all distributional predictors; zero-inflated models include the point mass |
| `twlss()` | Mean, power and dispersion vary; select `parameter = "power"` for the second link and `"scale"`, `"sigma"` or `"phi"` for the third |
| `shash()` | Skewness and tail weight matter; PIT checks remain useful when the package's deviance contrast is invalid |
| `ziP()` | Zero-inflated count probabilities include fitted zero mass; it is a different model from separate `ziplss()` predictors |
| `betar()` | Native simulation clips at epsilon endpoints, so diagnostics include their probability mass; this remains an approximation to the fitting likelihood |
| `scat()` | Scaled-t references retain the fitted heavy-tail parameters |
| `mvn()` | PIT checks each response separately; joint simulation retains covariance between responses |
| `mgcv::bcg()` and {mgcvUtils}'s `clognorm()` | Link extraction and response predictions are supported. See the help topic below for diagnostic support. |

For models with several distribution parameters, specify which link you want
when using `link()`, `inv_link()` or `extract_link()`. Here we recover the
Tweedie power and dispersion from their linear predictors, then select the
second predictor of a multivariate normal family:

```{r links}
inv_link(twlss(), parameter = "power")(0)
inv_link(twlss(), parameter = "phi")(0)
inv_link(mvn(d = 2), which_eta = 2)(1)
```

For the generalised extreme value (GEV) family, the mean exists when shape
is below one and the variance when shape is below one-half. If any fitted
mean is undefined, gratia retains the PIT and quantile panels and omits the
observed-versus-fitted mean panel. Signed deviance residuals also require
shape to be at least minus one. For sinh-arcsinh fits, use PIT or quantile
residuals if the deviance calculation fails because a fitted density exceeds
one. These checks use fitted probabilities and work even when deviance
residuals are undefined.

The [`diagnostic_support`](../reference/diagnostic_support.html) reference lists
the supported distributions and restrictions, including quasi families and
working correlations that do not define a joint response distribution.
